title: POC Weekly Sync - Reliability Incident Follow-up
summary: Weekly POC sync focused on the reliability incident that caused increased 5xx and 429 errors last Friday. Team reviewed preliminary logs, identified retry/backoff and client concurrency issues as likely contributors, discussed quick mitigations (client-side exponential backoff, reduce concurrency, increase timeouts) and longer-term fixes (routing to Dedicated pool, increase instance capacity, add circuit breaker, improved monitoring). Action items: customer to share correlated request IDs and example payloads; Redwood SE to run deeper log analysis, provide recommended timeout/retry config and a suggested rollback plan for the POC; schedule a bench test during low traffic window.
next_steps: StratoApps to upload example request logs + correlation IDs by 2026-03-08
Redwood SE (Daniel) to run detailed log analysis and recommended retry/timeouts by 2026-03-09
Schedule targeted bench run for production-like load on 2026-03-11 (low traffic window)
Samira to share pricing/impact of switching route to Dedicated pool by 2026-03-10

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-06
Time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Daniel Wu (Redwood SE), Rachel Lin (CTO, StratoApps), Marta Gomez (Platform Eng), Evan Cole (ML Eng), Jamal Price (SRE)

---
[00:00] Samira: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick recap — last week's POC run had a reliability incident on Friday where you saw a spike in 5xxs and 429s. we wanted to walk through what we know, go over logs you shared, and agree next steps. Rachel, do you want to start with a quick summary of what you saw?

[00:18] Rachel: Yeah, sure. thanks Samira. so, on Friday around 2pm our prod-ish environment hit a flurry of 5xxs, about 8 to 12% for a 20 minute window, and then we also saw a bunch of 429s after retries kicked in. we think some of it overlaps with a burst of concurrent requests from our frontend release, but it's hard to prove. we uploaded logs to the bucket, there's a zip w/ correlation ids — sorry some of the ids are truncated in the UI.

[00:41] Daniel: okay that's helpful. i skimmed the bundle earlier — thanks for that. initial look shows repeated client retries with small fixed backoff which likely exacerbated throttling. also saw a handful of longer tail latencies leading to timeouts upstream. question, do you have client-side timeout configured?

[00:55] Evan: right now our client lib has a 10s overall request timeout and retry policy is 3 retries with 500ms fixed delay. we've been conservative to reduce user facing errors but that may be fighting the server.

[01:08] Samira: that fixed delay plus concurrency is classic for creating retry storms; recommended is exponential backoff with jitter. we also want to check server-side timeouts — Redwood's default ingress timeout for the hosted path is 30s but if requests queue up because of CPU or KV cache misses you can still see increased 5xx.

[01:26] Marta: just to add, some requests are quite large — full document contexts — so tokenization/encoding time might also be part of the latency. we do also set the stream to wait for chunk completion, so there's additional buffering.

[01:42] Jamal: i pulled a prometheus dump from our side; there are clear spikes in concurrency correlated with the front-end deploy window. we also saw a rise in error rate from one specific route, /generate-chat, which maps to a single model variant.

[01:58] Daniel: that matches what i saw: the /generate-chat calls were hitting the model with longer seq lengths which increase per-token compute. Couple of quick mitigations: 1) reduce client concurrency or cap inflight per-user, 2) move that traffic to a dedicated routing pool if you need sustained throughput, 3) increase the client timeout slightly to avoid premature client retries that then cascade.

[02:20] Rachel: on dedicated — we wanted to understand cost tradeoffs, is Dedicated an immediate fix?

[02:26] Samira: Dedicated will give you predictable throughput and isolation, so it prevents noisy neighbor effects. cost depends on size of the reserved pool; i can send a ballpark. for the POC short-term we can also route only the heavy route to Dedicated and keep the rest on hosted to reduce cost.

[02:43] Evan: do you have a quick config you'd recommend for client retry/backoff? we've been using the default sdk settings.

[02:49] Daniel: recommended pattern — exponential backoff starting at 200-300ms up to a cap of 5s with full jitter, and a max of 3 total retries for idempotent calls. also, implement a circuit breaker on client side that opens after a short threshold so you don't hammer during server recovery.

[03:12] Marta: any recommended server side timeouts? we had an nginx layer with 60s timeout historically.

[03:18] Samira: for hosted path I'd suggest a 30-45s request timeout end-to-end; longer timeouts mean more queued work. We can also tune the model variant to a slightly smaller size if latency is critical — that can reduce per-token compute.

[03:33] Jamal: something we worried about — are retries idempotent? some of our requests are not strictly idempotent because they include side effects downstream in our system. so, reducing retries might increase user visible errors.

[03:45] Daniel: totally, for non-idempotent flows you should avoid auto retries and instead do an explicit server-side dedupe or client confirm pattern. If dedupe isn't possible, lower the retries and add user-visible queuing/UX.

[04:00] Rachel: we also noticed high 5xxs coming from a small subset of callers using an old sdk that doesn't include the new correlation header, which makes tracing hard. we'll reach out to the teams to patch but that won't be instant.

[04:14] Samira: please send those sdk versions and a few example requests; Daniel can map logs and isolate traces without the header but it's slower.

[04:22] Evan: one weird bit — we saw 502s with response body showing 'kvcache miss' in some snapshots, spelled in one of the logs as K-V cash miss, so i think some transcription or logging text is funky. could that indicate cold cache behavior?

[04:36] Daniel: yes, a KV cache miss means the model couldn't reuse previous key/value cache entries for autoregressive generation; cold cache results in higher compute and memory pressure. During bursts, if many cold sequences arrive, you can get latency spike and then 5xx if queues overflow. warm-up and caching is important.

[04:55] Rachel: is there a way to pre-warm the cache for common prefixes?

[04:59] Daniel: you can enable prefix caching for predictable prompts, and on our side we can increase warm pool capacity temporarily. also consider batching short requests to amortize overhead.

[05:12] Marta: what's the immediate low-friction change we can make this week to reduce the chance of another incident?

[05:16] Samira: short list — implement exponential backoff w/ jitter in client by EOD, reduce concurrent inflight per user to 3, temporarily route /generate-chat to Dedicated or a higher tier for the bench test window, and bump client timeout to 20s. those should materially reduce the retry storm risk.

[05:33] Jamal: ok let's agree — we'll do the client changes, and we will pick a low-traffic window for a controlled bench test. we'll push SDK updates to the teams that can do it quickly.

[05:46] Rachel: for the bench, we want Redwood to run a simulated production-like load against the POC so we can see if Dedicated removes the instability. can you scope that?

[05:54] Samira: yes, Daniel and i will set up a bench plan. typical approach: a 1-hour run that mimics your QPS and sequence length distribution. we can also vary concurrency to reproduce the failure mode.

[06:06] Daniel: i'll need 3 correlated request IDs and some representative payload sizes. also, tell me target QPS and percent of long sequence requests.

[06:15] Rachel: i'll get that uploaded. target QPS is 50 sustained with 8% long sequence (>1024 tokens) and the rest short-ish.

[06:25] Evan: any specific logging we should enable on our end? we currently capture latency, status codes, and basic headers.

[06:31] Daniel: add the full request+response size, client sdk version header, correlation id, and if possible the user id hash. that will let us map inflight behavior to model queues.

[06:42] Marta: regarding the 429 spike — does Redwood have built-in rate limit headers so we can backoff more intelligently?

[06:48] Samira: yes we expose X-RateLimit-Limit and X-RateLimit-Remaining on the hosted API; we also include Retry-After in some 429s. if you switch to Dedicated we'll provide stronger quota and per-route caps.

[07:02] Jamal: something else — when retries happened, we saw a sustained period of 5xxs that then slowly decayed; we need a circuit-breaker or automatic throttling rather than letting it slowly die.

[07:11] Daniel: agree. on client side add circuit-breaker and on server side we have graceful degradation features: route to a cheaper model if latency spikes, or automatically drop non-critical features. for the POC we can enable a fallback variant for that route.

[07:30] Rachel: fallback to a smaller model — does that change output quality? we have QA concerns.

[07:34] Samira: yes there is a tradeoff. fallback is to preserve availability; Redwood Optimize can help you track quality delta via prompt sets so you can quantify regressions. we can configure a canary to route, say, 10% to the fallback for evaluation.

[07:50] Evan: can we get the exact recommended client code snippet?

[07:54] Daniel: i'll post a sample in the notes — exponential backoff w/ jitter, circuit-breaker pseudo code, and a sample header set including correlation-id and sdk-version.

[08:03] Marta: for the log bundle — is there any PII we should scrub before upload?

[08:08] Samira: scrub user ids or replace with hashed ids. redact full utterances if they contain PII; we only need sizes and hashes for debugging.

[08:18] Rachel: timeline — we want to be confident by next Thursday for the next release. is that feasible?

[08:23] Samira: yes that's reasonable if we get logs by Monday and Redwood runs the bench Wednesday/Thursday. we'll aim for that cadence.

[08:33] Evan: quick question — were any 5xxs correlated to model OOMs?

[08:37] Daniel: not obvious in the log snippets, most errors were 502/503 from upstream timeouts/queue overflow. OOMs would show a more explicit error. i will verify in the deep dive.

[08:48] Jamal: do you have guidance on throttling behavior during autoscale events? our scaling sometimes lags and that causes short windows of pressure.

[08:55] Samira: Redwood Dedicated has configurable autoscale policies and burst capacity options; for hosted we can use routing and fallback features. we'll share recommended autoscale thresholds for your load profile.

[09:07] Rachel: any blockers for us to implement the immediate mitigations?

[09:10] Samira: no blockers from Redwood. main work is the SDK patch and log bundle. Daniel will supply the exact config.

[09:16] Daniel: i'll also produce a temporary client policy you can drop into the front end that limits inflight per user and the backoff. it should be a couple lines in your config.

[09:25] Samira: ok let's recap next steps and owners.

[09:28] Rachel: recap please.

[09:29] Samira: action items — Rachel to upload logs + correlation ids; Daniel to deep-dive and share retry/backoff and timeouts; Marta to run bench on 3/11; Samira to send Dedicated routing cost estimate. we'll reconvene after Redwood posts the bench results.

[09:46] Rachel: thanks everyone. appreciate the quick turnaround.

[09:50] Samira: thanks all. we'll follow up in the notes and Slack.

---
End of transcript.
